#4878. PlugShare finally adds dark mode, and there’s more for EV drivers

PlugShare is giving its EV charging app a big overhaul. Version 8.0 arrives worldwide for iPhone on November 10, with dark mode, a trip planner that shows how far apart charging stops are, and a rebuilt Apple Watch app that can point you to a charger compatible with your EV.

Dark mode was one of the most-requested features from PlugShare users. It works across the app and follows your iPhone’s settings, so if your phone switches to dark mode at sunset, your charging map will, too.

The trip planner gets a small but handy change. Each charging stop now shows how far it is from both the start of your trip and the previous stop. So when you’re deciding whether to stretch to the next fast charger or stop sooner, the number you need is right there.

PlugShare now loads your saved locations, trips, and profile when you open the app or sign in, so those tabs are ready to tap. You can also open and zoom in on station photos right from their thumbnails. That’s handy when you’re trying to figure out what corner a charging station is in in a big parking lot. The app also adapts its layout to the iPhone Duo’s different screens and folded positions.

The rebuilt Watch app lists nearby charging stations with distances and directions. It uses the filters you’ve set on your iPhone, so if you’ve filtered for plugs that fit your EV, that carries over to your wrist.

Tap a station and you’ll see its PlugScore, the network that runs it, a small map, and which plugs it has, including NACS, CCS, CHAdeMO, or J1772. The list refreshes when you raise your wrist and open the app. You can also add a shortcut to a round or corner slot on your watch face.

The iPhone update is rolling out through the App Store. PlugShare says Android users will get dark mode and a redesign based on Google’s Material 3 in early 2027.

#4877. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4876. How Emotions Shape Our Impressions of Others

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

This post was co-authored with Rebecca Schlegel, Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Texas A&M University.

What do you think of when you hear the word stereotype? This term has become highly polarizing in today’s society. It probably brings to mind ideas like social justice; diversity, equity, and inclusion training; meritocracy; oppression; wokeness; and equity. You probably have emotions about these ideas, possibly strong ones, and have attitudes about what we should do as a society about these things. But what comes to mind is probably not what psychologists mean when they study stereotypes, and people are often surprised by the role of emotions in shaping what we think about others.

When viewed through a psychological lens, stereotypes are not good or bad. They are byproducts of how people think. The human mind operates by creating categories or “bins” and using those bins to collect related information. As children learn language, for example, they might create a bin called “dogs,” and place everything that is four-legged and furry into that bin. This leads to some common errors, such as children calling a cat a “dog” because it is four-legged and furry. Typically, these errors are corrected by others (a parent explains it is not a dog, but a cat), and the categories get adjusted as children learn what information goes in what bin. This structure is critical for functioning in the world—we can enter a new situation and know what to expect because we’ve been in similar situations before. Without the category of “dog,” we would have to treat every encounter with a dog as a new experience. With the category of “dog,” we have some idea of how the animal will behave and what we should and shouldn’t do when encountering a dog, and we can talk with other people about our experiences with dogs to share information. Overall, categories help us learn faster and function better.

We use this same categorization process to make sense of the many different types of people we encounter in the world. From an early age, we learn categories and place people into those categories. We learn some bins at very young ages, such as family versus stranger. As we grow and learn, the categories are adjusted based on correcting errors and greater experience. Placing people into those categories allows us to quickly respond—children learn to treat someone in the bin of “stranger” very differently than they treat someone in the bin of “family.”

Stereotypes refer to the information and beliefs we put in the bins we have learned for groups of people. Just as people might associate the bin of “dog” with concepts like loyal or energetic, people associate bins for groups of people with different concepts. For example, people may associate the category of “football player” with concepts like “strong.” At their root, stereotypes are mental shortcuts that people use to make sense of other people just as they do with other types of categories in the world. Creating the bins and putting information in the bins is just a feature of how our brain makes sense of a complicated world.

The challenge comes when we develop emotions about the bins we use. One person might associate the bin of “dog” with loyalty and develop good feelings about dogs, whereas another person might associate the bin of “dog” with aggression and develop negative feelings about them. In the same way, people attach good or bad feelings to bins for categories of people. This process—where an emotion is attached to a category or idea—is called attitude formation. The bin is no longer neutral—there is an emotional tag that changes how you interact with the members of that category. If the bin of “dogs” is attached to negative feelings or fear, you avoid dogs. Similarly, you are disposed to act differently toward categories of people associated with negative emotions versus groups you associate with positive emotions. These emotions can be powerful guides to behavior.

The beliefs we hold about groups of people and the emotional responses we have toward the groups are different concepts in psychology. In daily life, however, these things often go hand in hand and are influenced by the messages we receive about groups. Societal views of smoking and smokers in the United States are an excellent example of how stereotypes (and the emotions they evoke) develop and can shift. From the 1920s through the 1960s, smoking was associated with glamor and wealth. This was the result of marketing by companies and striking images of celebrities in movies, ads, and television. Smoking was not only socially acceptable; it was a good thing—part of being a productive and engaged member of society. The group “smokers” had become associated with positive beliefs and positive emotions.

As the health consequences of smoking behavior and the resulting economic impact became clear, government officials took steps to change public perceptions of smoking. They banned cigarette advertisements, promoted anti-smoking campaigns, and prohibited companies from using terms that suggested particular brands were safer or healthy. Many of the campaigns were graphic and evoked strong emotion, such as images of smokers with cigarette burns in their clothes and yellowed teeth, diseased lungs, or people in wheelchairs struggling to breathe. These messages were not just providing information to people about the health risks—they were actively attempting to shift the stereotypes of smoking and smokers. Over time, “smokers” became associated with negative emotions and beliefs, and were viewed as dangerous, irresponsible, selfish, unhealthy, and disgusting. They were banned from restaurants, airplanes, workplaces, campuses, and stores.

In current society, there is a high level of concern and attitudes about stereotypes and what we should do about them. Stereotypes have become a focus of political debate and calls to action. However, from a psychological perspective, stereotypes exist because they are a byproduct of how people learn, think, and navigate a complex social world, and they cannot be removed. But we can understand how messages through advertising, media, and other sources affect the impressions we form about other people. Understanding how our impressions are formed can help all of us make more intentional evaluations about other people based on our own experiences and our personal values.

#4875. Humble Hauler autonomous trailer takes the truck out of trucking [update]

Less than a year after its founding, truckless trucking brand Humble Robotics has secured more than $75 million after a $51 million Series A funding round that will fuel the company’s transition from prototype to preproduction.

The latest funding round for the driverless, cab-less, and truck-less battery-electric freight platform developer was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from other existing investors Eclipse and Energy Impact Partners. Humble said it will use the funding for customer pilots, testing and validation, and early manufacturing.

“We’ve spent years proving that a truck can drive itself,” explains Humble Robotics founder and CEO, Eyal Cohen. “The harder question is how to make autonomy something a freight operator can depend on every day.”

We originally covered the Humble Hauler back in May. You can check out the original article, below, then let us know what you think of the company’s prospects in the comments.

The startup that dares to ask, “Why does the Macbook driving my freight around need a whole cab?” just showed off a fully driverless, cab-less, and truck-less battery-electric freight platform designed to handle containerized cargo more efficiently than ever.

Instead of looking at the tractor and asking how to make it work without a driver, Humble looked at the trailer, itself, redesigning the container chassis as a vehicle from the ground up. The end result isn’t just an autonomous solution, it’s an overall lighter platform without a cab that saves shippers the weight of a sleeper cab, a day cab, or the truck at all.

The Humble approach is said to improve payload efficiency of shipping containers, and intended for dock-to-dock operation.

“I have dedicated my career to building electric and autonomous vehicle technology,” explains Eyal Cohen, Humble Robotics’ founder and CEO. “For the first time, freight can be fully automated all the way to the loading dock. We are making freight sustainable, safe and efficient in a way no one thought was possible. And we’re doing it with an exceptional team of industry veterans and AV experts.”

Emerging from stealth after a $24 million funding round, Humble claims to have completed its first Humble Hauler prototype in less than six months – and they’ll soon be ready to begin autonomous testing in pilot programs with a number of logistics partners.

The vehicle uses a combination of cameras, lidar, and radar for 360-degree awareness (unhindered by seeing around a cab), and uses vision-language-action models to help the system respond to new scenarios.

Thanks to superior battery tech, a maturing global charging infrastructure, and a permanently damaged MidEast oil supply, there’s never been a better time to be an EV startup. Humble is hitting all the electric trailer buzzwords, too, while also touting the fact that the electric powertrain can reduce a company’s to volatile fuel prices even as it helps produce other cost benefits like lower maintenance costs.

There is a reason why the transportation industry developed separate cabs and trailers. Trailers can be loaded or unloaded for days and are much less expensive than trucks that serve both purposes in one piece. That allows the more expensive piece of the transport puzzle to be used more and allows the trailer to be loaded and unloaded while the cab is elsewhere working or in the shop. Query whether the savings they cite will surpass the costs of not having the flexibility of a cab and trailer design.

And if a robot like this can deliver on its promises without the baked-in inefficiencies of humanoids, they might be one step closer to provide that the most efficient solution to a problem is rarely a general one, and even rarer is it a solution that looks like a human.

#4874. Honda shows off its next electric motorcycle, and it’s wilder than you thought

Honda has been getting increasingly serious about electric motorcycles, but if you want to see just how weird the company thinks the future could get, take a look at the Honda EV Outlier Concept.

I got a chance to see the wild-looking machine in person at EICMA in Milan, where it looked like almost nothing else on the show floor. And that’s exactly the point.

The EV Outlier Concept originally debuted at last year’s Japan Mobility Show as Honda’s attempt to imagine an electric motorcycle that isn’t simply a conventional motorcycle with the engine swapped for a battery and motor. In fact, Honda describes the concept as looking toward the future of electric motorcycles beyond 2030.

Instead of a centrally mounted motor driving the rear wheel, the EV Outlier uses motors inside both wheels, giving it all-wheel drive and allowing Honda’s designers to completely rethink the rest of the motorcycle’s layout. The battery is housed in that large central black body, while the rider sits extremely low and behind it.

Honda describes the design philosophy with three words: “Gliding, Ecstasy, and Low.” The first refers to the smooth, nearly silent feeling of electric propulsion, while the second describes the instant acceleration and massive torque available from independently controlled front and rear motors. “Low” is more literal: Honda deliberately dropped the rider’s seating and eye position to create an entirely different sensation from a conventional motorcycle.

There’s even a bucket-style backrest designed to support the rider under hard acceleration and let the rider pivot through corners around their hips.

Cool and fun for Honda engineers to play with, but it seems a big no for reality, or at least a different road reality then mine.

Emergency tight swerves for accident avoidance? Nope, gone. Seeing even less of the road, even without a car in front of you, due to being so low? Not good for me nor the deer I don't avoid due to seeing it too late.

Unsprung mass due to hub motors - lots of literature on that topic, so I'll leave that alone.

Up front, traditional mirrors are replaced by cameras, while a wide digital cockpit can display things like lean angle, riding modes, front motor torque adjustment, and what the two wheels are doing in real time.

Will Honda actually build this thing? Almost certainly not exactly as you see it here. That’s what concepts are for.

But the EV Outlier is still interesting as a statement of intent. Honda is obviously still playing around with the freedom that electric drivetrains offer, and the company is asking what motorcycles could become once designers no longer have to work around engines, fuel tanks, transmissions, and traditional drivetrains.

And judging by what I saw at EICMA, Honda’s answer could get pretty wild.

#4873. ‘One-in-a-million’ yellow fish found in New York

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:22 AM EST

We’ll call him mellow yellow. An “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario in Upstate New York.

Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. To the naked eye, they appear scaleless, but are actually covered with tiny, almost microscopic scales. What they eat depends on their size. Smaller burbots will eat zooplankton, while bigger burbots prefer to snack on other fish.

The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey. It gets its unique color from a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism. A genetic mutation suppresses the normal pigmentation, it produces a yellow-orange appearance instead of the burbot’s usual grey, olive, or tan coloring. In wild fish, xanthochromism is less common than albinism or melanism, making this fish an “especially unusual capture.”

The burbot is a native species in the Great Lakes, but the USFWS team says the discovery highlights the effectiveness of the Service’s Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. The program uses a multi-gear fish-surveillance strategy to detect certain non-native species in the harbors, rivers, and embayments of the Great Lakes. Early detection of a watchlist species gives fisheries managers the best opportunity to implement prevention and removal measures if invasive species are detected. Since invasive species are often rare when they first enter new waters, the program uses electrofishing, fyke-netting, gill-netting, and environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to increase the chances that scientists detect an invasive species.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor,” the USFWS wrote in a statement. “It represents the first documented detection of a burbot during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few angler catches have been reported.”

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) fisheries biologists, who examined the fish and are familiar with the species, also observed that it was very thin and appeared to be in poor health. It was later sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis due to the “unexplained factors contributing to the continued suppression of its population”

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the burbot too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” the USFWS concluded.

#4872. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4871. CAT puts century-old train tech to work in its biggest underground machine yet

Diesel-electric locomotives have been barreling along America’s wide-open spaces for generations, and the century-old combination of highly efficient diesel engines spinning up generators to power high-torque electric motors has proven tough to beat. Now, Caterpillar is putting that century-old concept to work underground. Meet the CAT R3200 XE LHD.

One of the many hard-working machines moving chunks of Earth under your feet, an LHD (load, haul, and dump) machine is essentially a massive underground wheel loader designed to scoop up blasted rock, haul it through narrow mine tunnels, then dump it into trucks or ore passes. Built low and wide to fit in the tunnels, LHDs are workhorses of underground mining operations – and the new R3200 XE is CAT’s biggest yet, with a 25 ton payload and electric drive.

Before we get into the machine’s specs (the few that we have, anyway), I want to make sure understand that large-scale mining operations use obscene amounts of fuel, and a swing in site efficiency of just 1-2% can mean a huge difference in the bottom line – and fuel prices were up 27.4% (!) in August alone.

Keep the staggering weight of what that kind of fuel cost can mean to a fleet that buys fuel by the literal truckload as you read the rest of this.

Though not yet officially released by CAT, snippets of the company’s launch video have been leaking through dealers and trade journals, and they show the big machine powered by CAT’s newest 18.1 liter Tier 5 C18 diesel generator making 527 hp (~390 kW). That C18 reportedly sends electrons to the same electric drive system used in the company’s already successful 18-ton R2900 XE LHD.

In addition to a bigger generator and heftier payload, CAT says the upcoming R3200 XE LHD offers reduced cycle times versus the R2900 XE with 11% better speed on grade, plus reduced maintenance and repair costs thanks to design refinements for better durability, including redesigned axle. All told, that works out to 28% more tons per hour with 8% better fuel efficiency.

That efficiency is boosted by the same baked-in ADAS tech that’s made the smaller R2900 XE a favorite, and includes the latest version of CAT AutoDig and MineStar, ensuring that the machines are easy for experienced CAT operators to set up for remote, semi-autonomous, and even fully autonomous operation using Command for Underground.

We’ll post an update once CAT makes the full rundown of official specs public, which should be sooner rather than later. When that happens, we’ll see exactly how this big burrowing CAT stacks up against the competition from Sandvik, Epiroc, and Komatsu. In the meantime, let us know what you think of CAT’s newest electric drive machine in the comments.

#4870. A Forgotten Remedy for Depression

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Devon Frye

There’s growing concern about the risks of antidepressants, including side effects and withdrawal symptoms. Many people who are taking antidepressants are now turning to deprescribing resources, while others who are experiencing depression are wondering whether they should start taking antidepressants at all or if there’s another way.

But there’s one remedy that hasn’t gotten the attention it deserves: exercise.

In what follows, I’ll look at the surprising antidepressant effects of exercise, why it isn’t prescribed more widely, and a simple framework to help people get started.

One of the most astonishing findings in recent depression research is that exercise can be as effective as antidepressants, and some studies suggest it may be even more effective for mild to moderate depression. Millions of people have been prescribed powerful psychiatric drugs, often without being told that something as ordinary as walking, jogging, cycling, or strength training might provide comparable benefits.

The evidence has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Exercise ranks as one of the most effective known lifestyle interventions for depression. These include aerobic exercises, walking, jogging, strength training, and yoga. Intriguingly, evidence suggests that strength training is slightly more effective for women and younger adults, and yoga for men and older adults.

Exercise isn't just about shedding calories. It improves inflammation, metabolism, sleep, and the body's response to stress. These are precisely the factors that can go wrong in depression. But I think there's something deeper going on.

I've argued that depression may be a functional signal: our brain's way of telling us that something in our lives isn't going well and needs more attention. Sometimes the problem is a relationship, a job, or a life goal that no longer suits us. But sometimes the problem is the way we're living.

Humans evolved to move. Our ancestors spent much of their days walking, gathering food, carrying things, and engaging physically with the world. They didn't spend eight hours sitting in front of a computer, followed by another four hours staring at a smartphone. Yet that's how many of us live today.

Is it surprising that our bodies, and our minds, are protesting? Perhaps depression is telling us that something is wrong with the lives we've built for ourselves.

The evidence for the benefits of exercise is strong enough that a group of psychiatrists recently asked, in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, whether failing to prescribe exercise for depression could amount to “psychiatric malpractice.”

Part of the problem, they argue, is training. In one survey, 92 percent of mental health professionals said they'd received no formal training in prescribing exercise, and 41 percent said they never prescribe it at all.

Still, simply telling people to “be active” rarely works. People who struggle with depression need guidance and support.

For those for whom exercise is a real possibility, the same group offers a simple framework called FITT, which stands for frequency, intensity, time, and type. As a rule of thumb (and obviously to be adjusted for each person's physical health and other medical conditions):

But they also emphasize that less is better than none. Even one or two sessions a week, or 10 to 30 minutes at a time, can help.

Sometimes, what depression may be pointing to is precisely the mismatch between how we are designed to live and how we actually live. Exercise may be one way of answering its call.

#4869. 9-foot-tall Game Boy Color plays all the classics

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

The console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

“It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”

The giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art company Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

The two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

“It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez says. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”

From the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell says.

Fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

Meet the college student crafting electric guitars from scratch

This guy crammed a laptop into an Altoids tin

Clever kid builds phone charger powered by pet hamster

Teen brothers build a Disney-inspired ride in family basement

In Vermont, one man is bringing pay phones back to life

With goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity

Once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell says, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

Meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

When the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

The to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez says he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell says.

Alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”

In a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he said, he’s still mad.

Looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a new home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she says, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.

#4868. Polestar unveils Formula 2030 concept, previewing the next Polestar 2

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.

The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.

We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.

It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.

For context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar says the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.

The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.

Up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker says this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.

There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only shows itself when the car is driving autonomously.

The rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It says they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”

Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.

The interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.

But the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.

Polestar says it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the company’s head of interior design, put it plainly:

“As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”

That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.

The cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.

The four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.

The cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.

Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.

Now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.

What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four new models Polestar plans to launch in three years, and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.

Europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule. The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV.

Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this new head of design.

The proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, big haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

I have loved Polestar from the day they launched. Every car they design is a work of art and I love their commitment to transparency and sustainablitity. The 2023 Polestar 2 is still one of my favorite cars I've ever owned. I've driven the 3 and the 4 and both were fantastic. The fit and finish, ride and build quality, and NVH were all excellent. The upgraded 3 was probably going to be my next car in 2027 until they were forced to withdraw from the US. I think their future with the new 2 and 7 are bright and I'm still hoping (though I'm not holding my breath) that they will return to the US at some point. If the 5 was available here, I'd buy it today.

I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.

Polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.

Now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.

#4867. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4866. Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 12:01 PM EST

The world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables. This immense infrastructure is the foundation for much of the planet’s international power transmission and telecommunications, but marine biologists say the lines can provide an unexpected conservation benefit. With a bit of creative retooling, the ocean cables can also function as surprisingly good microphones for monitoring endangered whale populations.

“This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” said Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.

The latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work. In 2022, her team became the first researchers to demonstrate fiber-optic cable monitoring of blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus). The two species are respectively the largest and second-largest cetaceans, which also means they generate loud, ultra-low frequency vocalizations under 100 hertz. To record their calls, Bouffaut and colleagues utilized a system called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). The technique works by sending laser pulses through deep sea cables using specialized equipment, which researchers then analyze for miniscule sonic alterations caused by environmental sound waves. After pinpointing blue and fin whale communications, researchers then used the cables’ positions to map the marine mammals’ movements and population distribution.

Following her initial demonstrations, Bouffaut was curious if DAS could also work for other baleen whale species. The odds necessarily weren’t in her team’s favor—smaller species like the bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) and critically endangered North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) issue calls at much higher frequencies between about 150 and 300 hertz. Their vocalizations are also less intense and travel shorter distances, making them even more difficult to parse in DAS data.

In the spring, Bouffaut traveled to the town of Utqiaġvik on Alaska’s North Slope to collaborate with the local Indigenous Iñupiat community of whalers. She also partnered with Arctic broadband company Quintillion, who provided access to one of their own deep sea telecommunications cables. Amid terabytes of DAS recordings, Bouffaut eventually achieved another first in her field. She became the first person to confirm bowhead whale vocalizations by harnessing fiber-optic cables.

“Being able to detect bowhead whales on a telecommunication cable is the proof of concept we need to show that DAS can be used to monitor all baleen whales,” explained Bouffaut.

Although the new strategy isn’t sensitive enough to replace dedicated ocean monitoring using underwater microphone arrays, Bouffaut and her colleagues believe DAS could become an invaluable additional tool. It also showcases a way to convert existing infrastructures into multi-use systems.

“The review is also a call to action for scientists, industry partners and regulators to collaborate,” said Bouffaut. “We now have the technical blueprint to turn global undersea infrastructure into a global network for ocean conservation.”

#4865. Lucid says service wait times fell 20% after 40% jump in service staff

Lucid (LCID) says service wait times dropped 20% globally in the third quarter after it grew its technician and service-support staff by more than 40% in a single quarter.

The automaker is also adding Studio and Service Centers in Southern California, Los Angeles, Dallas, and the Chicago suburbs, plus 20 more Gravity Mobile Service vans. It’s a clear sign that service had become a problem for Lucid owners.

Lucid announced the numbers today, a day after its Q3 2026 earnings. Both comparisons are against the second quarter, not a year ago.

The hiring isn’t done either. After a 40%-plus increase in technicians, advisors, and concierges in Q3, Lucid wants that figure at 50% by the end of 2026 and 60% by Q1 2027. Mobile Service capacity in North America grew 15%, with a 40% target for year-end.

That’s a big hiring push for a company that laid off 18% of its workforce in June, its second cut in four months after a 12% reduction in February. Roughly 1,500 people left across those two rounds.

And owners noticed. On the LucidOwners forum, one Air Touring owner posted in early October that Lucid told them in writing to expect “a service time of about 7 weeks” at its Beverly Hills Service Center. Other threads blamed service-department layoffs for slow repairs and recall work.

Billy Hayes, Lucid’s Chief Customer Officer, said the company is “adding service personnel, and increasing Mobile Service capacity to reduce wait times and provide more convenient, responsive support.”

Here’s what’s opening, according to Lucid:

Lucid is also letting a growing number of its Certified Collision shops handle recall campaign work, which should take some pressure off its own Service Centers.

Outside the US, the expansion leans on partners. Munsterhuis Autobedrijven is Lucid’s first retail partner in the Netherlands (Hengelo), Cloppenburg Automobil SE opens a Duisburg retail and service site in January 2027, Autohaus Possögel starts authorized service in Naumburg, Germany, in December, and Emil Frey France will support Lucid’s launch in France. In Saudi Arabia, Lucid opened its first company-owned Body & Paint Repair Center in Riyadh, with more service sites in Riyadh and Dammam coming in the first half of 2027.

Lucid doesn’t say what the average wait time actually is.

A 20% drop from seven weeks is still more than five weeks. A 20% drop from one week is a non-issue. Without a baseline, owners can’t tell which one they’re getting.

It’s also hard to separate better service from fewer cars coming in. Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3, down 7% year-over-year, while it worked through inventory. Its fleet keeps growing, but slowly.

For context, Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3, five times Lucid’s volume, and it’s been leaning hard on mobile service too. Lucid is a much smaller operation trying to cover the US, Europe, and the Middle East with a thin network.

This is the right move, and it’s overdue.

Lucid has been one of the few EV startups with genuinely class-leading hardware. The Air’s efficiency is still unmatched and the Gravity is a great vehicle on paper, even if we found its software wasn’t ready. But when you’re asking someone to spend $80,000 or more on a car from a brand with an uncertain future, the ownership experience is half the sale. A seven-week wait for a repair kills that sale, and the referrals that come after it.

So growing service staff by 40% in a quarter is a big deal. It also tells you how thin those teams had gotten after two rounds of layoffs. Lucid cut too deep in the wrong place, and it’s now hiring to fix it.

The problem is the timing and the money. Lucid burned $1.04 billion in free cash flow in Q3 and only stays funded into late 2027 because the PIF just added another $1.75 billion. Meanwhile, the Midsize “Cosmos” that’s supposed to bring real volume doesn’t start production until the second half of 2027. Service is exactly where Lucid should spend between now and then, because the buyers it has today are the ones who’ll decide whether anybody trusts the brand with a cheaper EV.

#4864. Can a CAPTCHA Make You Think About God?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

You have done it hundreds of times. A grid of blurry squares appears; you click the ones with traffic lights, and you move on. Nobody has ever asked what was going through your mind while you proved you were not a robot.

In a paper just published in Behavior Research Methods, my colleagues and I used that same task to bring religious ideas to people's minds. Then we checked whether it actually worked.

For about 20 years, psychologists have been asking whether reminding people of God makes them more honest or generous. In his 2013 book Big Gods, Ara Norenzayan argued that belief in a god who watches and punishes helped strangers cooperate once societies grew too large for neighbors to monitor each other. Dominic Johnson had been making a related case since 2004, with more weight on the fear of punishment than on being watched, a point he later expanded in his book God Is Watching You. If either version is right, even a short reminder of God should change behavior in the lab.

The problem is the reminder itself. In implicit priming, participants unscramble sentences containing words like “divine” or “spirit,” in the hope that religious thoughts become active without anyone noticing. These primes are often too weak to demonstrate activation. In explicit priming, participants write a few sentences about God. This works, but many participants can guess what the study is about, and some then behave the way they think a good person should.

The findings have been messy as a result. A 2016 meta-analysis by Azim Shariff and his colleagues concluded that religious priming increases prosocial behavior. But when Michiel van Elk and his colleagues reanalyzed the same data in 2015, two different bias-correction methods yielded different answers: One suggested the entire effect could be explained by publication bias; the other suggested a real effect remained. Their conclusion was that meta-analysis alone cannot settle the question, and that only large, preregistered studies can. A 2024 meta-analysis by Shariff's research group added another twist: The association between religious belief and prosocial behavior appears mostly in what people say about themselves, and much less in what they do.

And almost none of these primes had ever been tested to see whether they really make people think about religion. We assumed they did.

Fırat Şeker, a former master's student of mine who is now pursuing his Ph.D. at UMass Amherst, and Ensar Acem, one of my current Ph.D. students and the manager of our MINT Lab at Kadir Has University in Istanbul, co-led a project to change this.

The idea was to hide the prime inside something people see every day. We built two versions.

In the grid version, participants saw a photo of an open book divided into 16 squares. A short phrase sat in one corner: “God sees,” “God punishes,” “God rewards,” or “God forgives.” The control group saw “He runs” in the same spot. Everyone was told to select the squares with no readable text, just as in an ordinary CAPTCHA.

In the keyword version, participants saw a picture of a Bible and had to pick the word that best described it. The right answer was “sacred,” hidden among options like “train,” “bed,” and “pencil.” The control group saw a photo of a table and had to pick “table” in the same way.

Then came the test. In a preregistered study of 2,770 American Christians, all participants completed a word-completion task. Participants saw fragments such as “f a i _ _” and filled in the blank, which could become “faith” or “faint.” Count the religious words people produce, and you have a behavioral measure of how easily religious thoughts come to mind. After that, participants played a standard dictator game, deciding how much of a small sum to share with a stranger. At the end, we asked them what they thought the study was about.

The explicit prime produced the strongest effect, as expected. But 11 percent of those participants correctly guessed the study's purpose.

The keyword version worked. When people had to find the word “sacred” under a picture of a Bible, they later produced more religious words than the control group did, and the same was true for the versions that pointed to a rewarding or a forgiving God. The version that pointed to a punishing God did not raise religious thoughts in general, but it did raise thoughts about sin and punishment specifically. Only 6 percent of these participants guessed what the study was about. The grid version did not work at all. We told people to select the squares without text, so they barely processed the sentence. A prime can be subtle, but it still needs a few seconds of attention.

Generosity did not change under any prime, including the explicit one. The experimental record here is mixed. In 2018, Joseph Billingsley and his colleagues found that an explicit prime increased giving in a dictator game while an implicit prime did not, and Cristina Gomes and Michael McCullough had found no effect of implicit priming on the same game in 2015. The meta-analytic picture depends on how one corrects for publication bias, as van Elk and his colleagues showed. So a null result is not out of line with what others have found. There is also a design reason. Norenzayan’s point in Big Gods was that religion works when it is in the situation, at the moment a person decides. In our study, the word-completion task came between the prime and the game, so by the time people chose how much to give, the reminder may already have faded. But when a religious prime fails to affect behavior in future studies, researchers can now rule out the most boring explanation: that the prime never reached anyone in the first place.

There is now a tested, low-suspicion method for activating religious thoughts in online studies. It has separate primes for punishing, rewarding, and forgiving images of God. That separation matters. Researchers disagree about whether it is the feeling of being watched or the fear of punishment that makes religious people behave better, and until now there was no clean way to pull the two apart. The materials and data are freely available on OSF.

Almost 10 years ago, Hasan G. Bahçekapili and I argued in Religion, Brain and Behavior that the question “Is religion necessary for morality?” has an easy answer: no, since plenty of people are moral without any religious belief. The harder question, and the one that remains unsolved, is how religion transforms morality once it enters the picture, in our evolutionary past, in history, and in the life of a single person. One reason it stayed unsolved is that we could not trust our own manipulations. Some questions that were put aside as unanswerable may only have been waiting for better tools. The same trick should also work outside religion, for anything that fits in the corner of a picture.

Everyone has heard of the replication crisis in psychology. Its sibling, the validity crisis, gets much less attention. In 2021, David Chester and Emily Lasko reviewed the experimental manipulations used in social psychology and found that most had never been tested to see whether they changed what they were supposed to change. A result can replicate perfectly and still be about nothing in particular.

Validation studies are not glamorous and rarely make the news. But before we ask whether God makes people good, we need to be sure that we have actually made them think about God. The field needs many more studies like this one, and far fewer assumptions.

Bahçekapili, H. G., & Yilmaz, O. (2017). Is religion necessary for morality? Religion, Brain & Behavior, 7(4), 279–281. https://doi.org/10.1080/2153599X.2016.1249924

Billingsley, J., Gomes, C. M., & McCullough, M. E. (2018). Implicit and explicit influences of religious cognition on Dictator Game transfers. Royal Society Open Science, 5(8), 170238. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.170238

Chester, D. S., & Lasko, E. N. (2021). Construct validation of experimental manipulations in social psychology: Current practices and recommendations for the future. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 16(2), 377–395. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691620950684

Johnson, D., & Krüger, O. (2004). The good of wrath: Supernatural punishment and the evolution of cooperation. Political Theology, 5(2), 159–176. https://doi.org/10.1558/poth.2004.5.2.159

Johnson, D. (2015). God Is Watching You: How the Fear of God Makes Us Human. Oxford University Press.

Gomes, C. M., & McCullough, M. E. (2015). The effects of implicit religious primes on dictator game allocations: A preregistered replication experiment. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(6), e94–e104. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000027

Kelly, J. M., Kramer, S. R., & Shariff, A. F. (2024). Religiosity predicts prosociality, especially when measured by self-report: A meta-analysis of nearly 60 years of research. Psychological Bulletin, 150(3), 284–318. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000413

Norenzayan, A. (2013). Big Gods: How Religion Transformed Cooperation and Conflict. Princeton University Press.

Shariff, A. F., Willard, A. K., Andersen, T., & Norenzayan, A. (2016). Religious priming: A meta-analysis with a focus on prosociality. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 20(1), 27–48. https://doi.org/10.1177/1088868314568811

Şeker, F., Acem, E., Vurgun, R., Dogruyol, B., Isler, O., & Yilmaz, O. (2026). Divine verification: Introducing a CAPTCHA-based religious priming technique. Behavior Research Methods, 58, 316. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03147-1

van Elk, M., Matzke, D., Gronau, Q. F., Guan, M., Vandekerckhove, J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2015). Meta-analyses are no substitute for registered replications: A skeptical perspective on religious priming. Frontiers in Psychology, 6, Article 1365. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01365

Yilmaz, O., & Bahçekapili, H. G. (2015). Without God, everything is permitted? The reciprocal influence of religious and meta-ethical beliefs. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 58, 95–100. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2015.01.003

#4863. Chunky mama bear wins 2026 Nope award for quick retreat from bigger rival

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 11, 2026 1:12 PM EST

Despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she said, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.
